subject: Interconnect isolation, sidecar controls & attack-path summary - RFI
messages:

Subject: RFI follow-up: need a clear isolation model for inter-account peering

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks again for the demo last week. Umbratek's security review team asked for a concise description of how Redwood isolates tenant workloads when customers use dedicated capacity that must communicate with our shared control plane and with other cloud services. Specifically they want: a short network diagram, explanation of data-plane/control-plane separation, allowed interconnect patterns (VPC Peering, PrivateLink, Transit Gateway), and an attack-path summary that covers KV cache poisoning, lateral movement from sidecars, and inter-tenant co-residency risks.

Could you send a short narrative and any diagrams we can attach to the RFP (we'll include them in the security appendix)? We need a version vetted by your security lead if possible.

Appreciate it — David

--
David Li
Senior Security Architect
Umbratek Systems

From: kimberly_park@redwood.ai
To: David Li <d.li@umbratek.com>
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.ai, secops@umbratek.com
Date: Sun, 12 Jul 2026 11:02:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: RFI follow-up: need a clear isolation model for inter-account peering

David —

Thanks, we've put together an initial packet (attached) and a short attack-path summary below. Sean Gallagher (cc: internal) is our security lead and will add the vetted threat-model details and a refined diagram. For the RFP appendix we recommend using the attached diagram named "redwood-interconnect-diagram-v3.svg" (it has layers turned on for control/data plane).

High-level narrative (for your appendix):
- Control plane: logically separated service endpoints in our control VPC; all management traffic is mutually authenticated with mTLS and signed tokens. Customers using Dedicated capacity connect their compute VPCs via isolated peering constructs or AWS PrivateLink endpoints; control-plane writes are only allowed over customer-authenticated channel and are rate-limited per account.
- Data plane (inference): runs in dedicated GPU pools when customer purchases Dedicated. Networking uses tenant-scoped subnets and strict security groups. We support two interconnect patterns: 1) Customer-managed VPC peering with explicit route controls and prefix lists that limit access to Redwood serving endpoints; 2) PrivateLink-style interface endpoints that preserve address-space separation and avoid route table changes. Transit Gateway is available for enterprise customers who require centralized routing; we recommend Transit with segmented route tables per tenant to avoid broad route propagation.
- KV/prefix cache: cache instances are either per-tenant (dedicated) or strongly namespace-scoped for shared pools. All cache update operations require signed requests from the serving runtime; cache entries incorporate a namespace prefix + HMAC to reduce cross-tenant collision risk.

Attack-path summary (short):
- KV cache poisoning: attack requires forging signed cache update requests or leaking the per-tenant HMAC key. Mitigations: per-tenant keys, strict auth, immutability windows for cached prompts, and proactive integrity checks that compare candidate cache content to canonical store.
- Sidecar lateral movement: sidecars run with minimal privileges; we use Linux seccomp profiles, cgroups, and network policies to restrict outbound flows. Sidecars cannot modify serving binaries or kernel modules. Ephemeral workloads (batch) are scheduled on separate node pools where possible.
- Co-residency in shared pools: shared GPU pools are isolated at process and namespace level via container runtime and enforce seccomp, AppArmor, and cgroup limits. We recommend Dedicated pools for highest isolation requirements.

Attachments: redwood-interconnect-diagram-v3.svg, isolation-matrix-umr.xlsx, attack-paths-and-mitigations.pdf

Hope this helps for the appendix. Sean will follow up with a short threat-model appendix you can quote verbatim.

Best,
Kimberly Park
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

From: sean_gallagher@redwood.ai
To: David Li <d.li@umbratek.com>, kimberly_park@redwood.ai
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Date: Sun, 12 Jul 2026 13:20:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: RFI follow-up: need a clear isolation model for inter-account peering

David — attaching a concise threat-model summary you can include in the RFP appendix. Quoted below are three representative attack paths with likelihood and mitigations. Please let us know if you'd like these expanded into a table for your procurement team.

--- Attack path A: KV cache poisoning (Likelihood: low-medium) ---
Scenario: An attacker with code-execution in a co-resident tenant attempts to push malicious cached prefixes to influence generation results for another tenant.
Prereqs: ability to craft signed cache-update requests or compromise runtime signing keys.
Controls: per-tenant cache namespaces + HMAC key rotation (daily by default for shared pools), signed cache-update endpoints, integrity monitoring that correlates cached entries with canonical prompt store, alerting for cache-hotkey anomalies, automatic cache quarantining when anomalous updates detected.
Residual risk: low when keys are rotated and integrity checks operate normally; recommend Dedicated pools for high-sensitivity workloads.

--- Attack path B: Sidecar exfiltration via permissive host networking (Likelihood: low) ---
Scenario: Malicious sidecar uses host networking to access instance metadata or neighbor processes to escalate.
Controls: container runtime enforces network namespace isolation; metadata access requires instance profile restrictions and IMDSv2 where applicable; eBPF-based egress policies log unexpected flows and trigger ephemeral network block.
Residual risk: low with enforced IMDSv2 and egress logging; additional hardening available for on-prem customers.

--- Attack path C: Control-plane impersonation (Likelihood: rare) ---
Scenario: Compromise of customer-managed credentials used by control-plane agents to perform deployments leading to unauthorized configuration changes.
Controls: mutual TLS for control-plane channels, short-lived provisioning tokens, customer-managed KMS/HSM integration for signing, RBAC and approval workflows in Console, immutable audit trail forwarded to customer SIEM.
Residual risk: mitigated-to-low with customer KMS and 2-person approvals for sensitive rollout.

Attached: attack-paths-and-mitigations.pdf (contains more detail, sequence diagrams).

- Sean Gallagher
Security Lead | Redwood Inference

Thanks Sean/Kim — this is exactly what we needed. A couple quick clarifying questions before we finalize the appendix:
1) For the HMAC-based cache namespace scheme, can you confirm whether keys are customer-specific (i.e., per-account) even in shared pools, or are they per-node? We prefer per-account secrets.
2) In the event of a suspected cache-poison event, what is the operational playbook (who we call, expected MTTI/MTTR, and whether you will roll-forward or quarantine)?

If you can reply with two short bullets we can close the RFI. We'll also link to the Drive diagram you attached in our submission.

-David
